facts.statement: Ceratosuchus was an extinct alligatorine crocodile that lived in the latest Paleocene and earliest Eocene epochs in North America.
facts.quote: Ceratosuchus ("horned crocodile") is an extinct genus of alligatorine crocodylian from latest Paleocene rocks of Colorado's Piceance Basin and earliest Eocene rocks of Wyoming's Bighorn Basin in North America

facts.statement: The genus name Ceratosuchus refers to the pair of flattened, triangular bony plates extending from the back of its head.
facts.quote: It is named for the pair of flattened, triangular bony plates that extend from the back of its head.

facts.statement: The discovery began when Theodore Burdosh found a knob of bone projecting from a piece of rock during an expedition.
facts.quote: Fortunately, a knob of bone projecting from an otherwise undistinguished piece of rock had caught the eye of Mr. Burdosh, and the block had been broughtto the Museum.

facts.statement: K. P. Schmidt named the genus Ceratosuchus in 1938 based on a skull found in Colorado.
facts.quote: Ceratosuchus was named in 1938 by K. P. Schmidt for a skull from Colorado.

facts.statement: University of Michigan paleontologists recovered further remains from Wyoming, which were described by William Bartels in 1984.
facts.quote: Further remains, including additional skulls, mandibles, and cervical armor, was recovered from Wyoming by University of Michigan paleontologists and described by William Bartels in 1984.

facts.statement: Ceratosuchus had a moderately-sized skull notable for horns formed by the expansion of the squamosal bones at the rear corners of the skull roof.
facts.quote: The skull, of a moderately-size alligatorine, is most notable for its horns, formed by expansion of the bones (squamosals) that formed the rear corners of the skull roof.

facts.statement: The horns of Ceratosuchus were bulbous and pointed upward.
facts.quote: These horns were bulbous and pointed up.

facts.statement: Ceratosuchus had five teeth in the premaxilla, fifteen in the maxillae, and twenty in the dentaries.
facts.quote: There were five teeth in both of the bones that made up the tip of the snout (premaxilla), fifteen in the paired maxillae that formed the sides of the upper jaw, and twenty in both dentaries of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The front of the lower jaw was flattened with spade-like teeth pointing partially forward.
facts.quote: The front of the lower jaw had a flattened shape, and the teeth located here pointed partially forward, with a spade-like form.

facts.statement: The lower jaw teeth varied in shape, with the first thirteen being pointed and the last seven ranging from spatulate to globular.
facts.quote: The teeth had variable shapes; the first thirteen teeth in the lower jaw were pointed, while the last seven graded from a spatulate shape to a large globular shape.

facts.statement: William Bartels proposed that the small size and bluntness of the horns made them unlikely weapons or tools for threat displays.
facts.quote: Bartels proposed that the horns' small size and bluntness made them unlikely weapons, and their small size also made use in a threat display unlikely.

facts.statement: Bartels suggested the horns were used for species recognition to distinguish Ceratosuchus from Allognathosuchus.
facts.quote: Instead, he favored their use as signals for species recognition: in this case, the horns would allow Ceratosuchus and species of Allognathosuchus to tell each other apart.

facts.statement: Fossils of Ceratosuchus have been found in overbank mudstone deposits.
facts.quote: Ceratosuchus is known from overbank mudstone deposits.

facts.statement: William Bartels reported that only 5% of Clarkforkian crocodilian specimens collected by the University of Michigan could be certainly assigned to Ceratosuchus.
facts.quote: Bartels reported that only 5% of Clarkforkian crocodilians collected by the University of Michigan can be certainly assigned to Ceratosuchus

facts.statement: Bartels proposed that skull morphology and tooth wear indicate Ceratosuchus was a generalist predator of various invertebrates and vertebrates.
facts.quote: Instead, he proposed that skull morphology and tooth wear better fit generalized predation on a variety of invertebrates and vertebrates.

facts.statement: Ceratosuchus lived between 57.5 and 51.1 million years ago during the Thanetian to Ypresian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Thanetian to Ypresian (57.5 to 51.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: Traditional interpretations suggest the blunt posterior teeth were for feeding on mollusks or turtles, though Bartels noted the animals were too small for large bivalves or non-juvenile turtles.
facts.quote: Although the blunt posterior teeth of Allognathosuchus and Ceratosuchus have been traditionally interpreted as for feeding on mollusks or turtles, Bartels noted that these crocodilians were too small to feed on large bivalves or non-juvenile turtles, and that modern crocodilians usually swallow snails whole.
